What are the six pillars of the Well-Architected Framework?

Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization and Sustainability. They are not trade-offs to arbitrate but a synergy. For security, the principles include a strong identity foundation, traceability, defense at every layer, automation, protecting data in transit and at rest, and preparing for incidents. I link these areas to the course domains: IAM, detection, infrastructure, data and incident response.
6 pillars
What is the AWS Well-Architected Tool used for?

It is a free tool to review a workload against the six pillars. You choose the workload, answer questions, the tool identifies high and medium risks and provides advice, videos and documentation, then you generate a report and track progress with milestones. It is declarative: it is based on my answers, not on an automatic inspection.
What is AWS Audit Manager and how does it collect evidence?

Audit Manager continuously assesses the risk and compliance of my workloads to prepare for audits. I choose a prebuilt framework (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR, CIS) or a custom one, I define the scope, and it automatically collects evidence from CloudTrail, Config, Security Hub and License Manager. I can add manual evidence and delegate reviews, then generate a report with links to the evidence. It works multi-account with Organizations.
What is the difference between Audit Manager and AWS Artifact?

Audit Manager collects the evidence of MY controls in MY accounts. AWS Artifact provides the compliance reports of AWS itself (certifications, attestations) and certain agreements. In the shared responsibility model, Artifact documents AWS's part and Audit Manager helps prove mine.

CloudFormation describes infrastructure as code; used well, it makes deployments reproducible and controllable (least privilege, protection of critical resources, secrets kept out of the template, drift detection).

Service role: deploy without giving rights to the developer
AWS CloudFormation
The developer calls CloudFormation with the template and passes the service role. They only have cloudformation:* and iam:PassRole rights on THIS role.
CloudFormation assumes the service role: it is the one that will act on the resources, on behalf of the user.
The create, update and delete operations on the stack's resources are performed with the role's permissions (here s3:*Bucket).
The developer has no direct S3 permission: least privilege is respected. They can deploy the stack but not handle the bucket by hand.
Developer permissions: deploy and pass ONE specific role
CloudFormation rights: create, update, delete and describe stacks.
Without iam:PassRole, the user cannot give the service role to CloudFormation.
We limit to one specific role (least privilege) instead of *.
The role can only be passed to the CloudFormation service, not to EC2 or Lambda.
Can the user directly create an S3 bucket with s3:CreateBucket?
Their policy grants no S3 permission: only the service role has it.
Can the user pass another role (e.g. AdminRole) to CloudFormation?
PassRole is limited to cfn-s3-service-role.
Service role trust policy: only CloudFormation can assume it
The principal is the CloudFormation service.
Role assumption action; the actual permission to create buckets is in another policy, attached to the role.
Can a human assume this role directly with this trust policy?
The authorized principal is cloudformation.amazonaws.com, not a user.
